proseFields.Airbags: Not visible as deployed — steering wheel area and passenger fascia appear intact in the interior shots, seats and trim are undisturbed, and the impact height (wheel/bumper level) is consistent with non-deployment. Confirm steering wheel centre and curtain trim on inspection.
proseFields.Red Flags:
- Category S on a near-new car: the structural trigger is almost certainly behind the struck front corner (chassis leg / inner wing) — not visible in the photos. Budget posture must assume possible jig/pull work until inspected.
- EV-specific: underfloor HV battery integrity is unverifiable from photos. Any casing damage transforms the economics entirely. The green HV warning stickers confirm the yard is treating it as live high voltage.
- Cluster shows service wrench and park-assist failure; with the 12V/HV systems powered the fault picture looks limited, but a full diagnostic scan is needed — ADAS (front camera visible at windscreen) will need calibration after front-end repair.
- Cat S V5 process: the buyer must apply to DVLA for a replacement V5, which will be permanently marked Category S and will show on all future HPI checks — a permanent resale value impact.
- Parts availability risk on a model this new: lead times on OEM front-end components could extend the repair timeline significantly.
proseFields.Bidder Note: Near-delivery-mileage current-generation EV with a repairable but genuinely structural front corner — the margin case is strong only if the chassis leg and HV battery check out. No previous salvage auction history — this appears to be a first write-off.

proseFields.Confidence Level: Medium — good photo coverage and a corroborated odometer, but the structural extent behind the struck corner and the HV battery condition are unverifiable remotely.
proseFields.Key Cost Drivers:
1. Suspension corner rebuild plus structural verification — the destroyed wheel confirms heavy load through the suspension; if the chassis leg behind that corner needs jig work, labour rises materially.
2. LED headlamp and bumper assembly on a current-generation model — used/breakers supply for a 2025/26 ë-C3 Aircross is very thin, so OEM pricing may be unavoidable on several lines.
3. EV high-voltage system inspection/certification before and after repair — a fixed overhead irrespective of panel costs.
proseFields.Exit Band Position: mid-high — near-delivery mileage, current-generation top-trim EV (strong desirability) offset by confirmed single-corner structural damage on a Cat S.
proseFields.Margin Calculation: The band position reflects a high-desirability vehicle carrying moderate-to-heavy structural damage: newness and trim pull the exit position up, the Cat S corner strike holds it back from the top step. The repair is a moderate-to-heavy job — a full suspension corner rebuild, front-end panel and lamp replacement, plus paint and ADAS calibration — with the cost ceiling driven by two binary unknowns: whether the chassis leg needs jig work and whether the HV battery is untouched. If both resolve favourably, the itemised repair total against a near-new EV's exit position should leave a workable margin; if either goes the wrong way, the economics deteriorate quickly. Bid accordingly: price the visible repair, hold a contingency for the structural unknown, and treat the HV battery as a walk-away condition if inspection raises doubt.
proseFields.Recommended Action: Book a £10 Copart WhatsApp video inspection (48hrs before sale minimum) — significant unknowns remain that a visual inspection can answer; see checklist below. Do not commit a bid price until the chassis leg and HV battery questions are addressed.
proseFields.Realistic Exit Value: Desirability is exceptional: a 2026-registered, current-generation ë-C3 Aircross in top Max Extended Range trim with 2,681 miles — effectively a delivery-mileage car, which per the newness principle overrides the usual EV battery-anxiety penalty. The live market matrix (retail £23,030–£26,023; trade £19,576–£22,119 at this mileage, Copart-listed source) frames a strong underlying value base. Against that, the damage is materially structural — a wheel-destroying corner strike with confirmed suspension failure and a Cat S rating implying chassis leg involvement — though mitigated by the car running and driving, no airbag deployment, and an undisturbed engine bay and interior. The two signals pull in opposite directions: top-tier desirability versus moderate-to-heavy single-corner structural damage. That nets out one step above the middle of the Cat S band rather than the top of it.
proseFields.Visible Damage Summary:
Confirmed body style: 5-door SUV/hatchback (Citroën ë-C3 Aircross, two-tone white/black roof). Windscreen sticker suffix: X (insurance company vendor, low value category) — write-off status is set by the listed Category S, not the sticker.

This is a front corner impact on a near-delivery-mileage electric vehicle (2,681 miles, dash photo corroborates the listed odometer exactly). The front bumper assembly is completely detached/removed, exposing the bumper reinforcement bar, radiator pack and lower under-tray across the full front. The structural damage footprint, however, is concentrated on one front corner: the wing on the struck side is deformed with the arch liner destroyed, and the front wheel at the damaged corner is shredded to destruction — alloy broken apart, tyre completely delaminated — with the wheel sitting visibly collapsed/displaced in the arch, confirming suspension component failure at that corner. The opposite front flank, wing and lamp are undisturbed. Damage zone classification: front corner — impact event, strike-height band low (bumper/wheel/sill height).

Headlamp status: the headlamp on the struck corner cannot be confirmed serviceable — the bumper is detached, the lamp mounting recess is exposed and the unit appears displaced from its mounts. The lamp on the opposite corner appears intact and seated.

The engine bay photo shows the high-voltage power electronics, orange HV cabling and coolant systems visibly intact and undisturbed — no displacement is visible. The cluster shows READY with drive engaged ("DRIVES" yard annotation corroborates the Run and Drive designation), but displays "Front Park Assist sensor failure", a TPMS warning, a service wrench and a battery-charge related telltale — consistent with the missing bumper (sensors live in the bumper skin) and destroyed wheel.

Secondary damage: rear flank scuffing and scratches around the rear quarter, rear lamp area and rear bumper corner on one side — mid-height cosmetic abrasion, separate from the front impact and treated independently. The charge port flap in the rear quarter is missing/broken, exposing the flap mechanism. Roof, glass and tailgate appear undamaged; interior is clean and unworn, consistent with the mileage.

Bumper reinforcement bar: present and exposed; possible deformation at the struck end — not clearly confirmed on its own shots, flagged below. Bonnet: appears largely intact; leading-corner alignment at the struck side worth checking, no clear deformation visible. Chassis leg behind the struck corner: not directly visible — given the Cat S rating with a wheel-destroying corner strike, intrusion into the chassis leg/inner wing behind that corner is the most likely structural trigger; this is a hypothesis to confirm on inspection, not a certainty.
proseFields.Alternative Damage Scenario: The photos are consistent with the listing: a single front-corner impact (likely kerb/island or low object strike at speed) destroying the wheel and suspension, with the bumper subsequently stripped for assessment. The rear flank scuffing and missing charge flap are a separate, minor event — possibly post-accident handling or a prior car-park scrape — and should not be folded into the front impact narrative.
proseFields.WhatsApp Inspection Checklist:
1. Show the chassis leg and inner wing behind the damaged front corner from below and inside the arch — look for creasing, folding or weld-line distortion (the Cat S trigger).
2. Show the damaged-side front wheel and suspension close up to confirm which components have failed — strut, lower arm, hub carrier, driveshaft — and whether the subframe mount is disturbed.
3. Show the underside of the floor from the front, focusing on the HV battery casing edges and any orange cabling runs — look for gouges, dents or cracked casing.
4. With the vehicle in READY, ask the handler to confirm it engages drive and reverse and rolls (on the good wheels), and to pan slowly across the full instrument display so every warning message can be read.
5. Show the bumper reinforcement bar end-on at the struck side to confirm whether it is bent, and the radiator/condenser pack faces for impact damage or leaks.
6. Show the struck-corner headlamp unit close up — mounting tabs, lens and rear connectors — to confirm whether it is reusable or requires replacement.
7. Confirm the bonnet opens, closes and latches correctly, and show the panel gaps along the leading edge on the damaged side.
8. Inspect and photograph all four wheels and tyres close-up — confirm no shredding, kerbing, cuts or bulges (the listing photos do not show the wheels clearly enough to confirm condition)
